region: Verzenay · Montagne de Reims, Champagne, France
about: The Godmé family have been vignerons in Verzenay, a Grand Cru village on the northern flank of the Montagne de Reims, since the nineteenth century. Hugues Godmé’s grandfather Joseph began bottling the family’s own Champagne after the Second World War. Hugues was given his first vineyard in 1976, when he finished viticulture school. He later broke with family tradition by abandoning chemical treatments in 2006 and moving to organic and then biodynamic farming. Today he works with his wife Dominique and their daughter Lucille, the fifth generation, on about seven and a half hectares.

The Blanc de Noirs is pure Pinot Noir from the Grand Cru villages of Verzenay and Verzy, where cool, north-facing chalk slopes give Pinot Noir firm structure and a mineral edge. Each parcel is pressed and fermented separately with native yeasts, and about 40 percent of the wine is fermented in neutral oak barrels. Wines from the current harvest are blended with reserve wines from the two previous years. The second fermentation and aging take place in the family’s chalk cellar beneath a Verzenay vineyard, where the wine rests at least three years before release.

In the glass it is a pale gold blanc de noirs that leans toward red fruit and chalk rather than richness. Wine Spectator’s Alison Napjus found ripe green apple and blackberry carried by firm acidity, finishing on almond and anise, while John Gilman noted white peach, apple and limestone. Peter Liem, in his book Champagne, describes the house’s Blanc de Noirs as having “vivacious structure and dark, mineral-driven fruit,” built on finesse as much as power.
facts: 100% Pinot Noir, Grand Cru Verzenay and Verzy
Current harvest with reserve wines from the two prior years
Traditional method; about 40% fermented in neutral oak
At least 36 months on the lees
